analysis.one_liner: Gives carmakers a doubled tax deduction for factory wages and rolls back federal emissions and fuel-economy rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2025 and referred to two House committees, where it has sat with no vote or hearing since; it has 16 cosponsors (15 Republicans, 1 Democrat).
analysis.plain_summary: The bill creates a tax deduction worth twice the wages automakers pay factory workers — but only for companies that meet a list of conditions, including keeping production in the United States, providing platinum-level health coverage and pensions, sharing profits when they buy back stock, and staying neutral in union organizing drives. At the same time, it wipes out the 2024 federal emissions and fuel-economy rules for cars and trucks, takes away California's power to set stricter car standards, and requires replacement rules that cannot push automakers toward electric vehicles.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic auto manufacturers gain a large tax deduction and freedom from the 2024 emissions and fuel-economy standards, plus relief from California's stricter rules. Auto workers can gain if their employers choose to qualify, since the deduction is only available to companies paying high wages with strong health and retirement benefits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic auto manufacturers and some factory workers

how_it_helps.text: Automakers that keep 75% of vehicle assembly and parts production in the U.S. can deduct 200% of their factory wages, subject to a $150,000-per-worker cap, and can also subtract those wages from the income used to calculate the corporate alternative minimum tax.

The deduction is only available to companies that offer platinum-level health coverage, a pension replacing at least 50% of pay after 30 years or a 10% 401(k) contribution, at least $2,000 in profit-sharing for every $1 billion in buybacks or special dividends, and neutrality during union organizing efforts.

The bill voids the EPA's 2024 greenhouse gas rules for light-, medium-, and heavy-duty vehicles and NHTSA's 2024 fuel-economy rules for model year 2027 and later, and revokes California's waivers, including its zero-emission vehicle mandate, while repealing other states' ability to adopt California's standards.

It directs agencies to write new standards based on economic practicability, and bars the greenhouse gas standards from requiring, directly or indirectly, the production or sale of electric vehicles; the CAFE and emissions standards are also deemed satisfied if a manufacturer complies with either one.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the tax deduction through reduced corporate tax revenue. Car buyers and drivers bear higher lifetime fuel costs as fuel-economy rules loosen, and everyone bears more tailpipe pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. California and the states that follow its standards lose their stricter vehicle rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Taxpayers, drivers at the gas pump, and California

drawbacks.text: The tax deduction would reduce federal revenue both directly and by lowering the income subject to the corporate alternative minimum tax, with no offsetting revenue in the bill.
Repealing the 2024 fuel-economy and emissions standards means vehicles burn more gasoline and emit more pollution over their lifetimes, raising drivers' fuel costs and contributing to climate change.
Revoking California's waiver, including its zero-emission vehicle mandate, and repealing Section 177 strips stricter standards from every state that had adopted them.

The worker protections are entirely conditional: a company only gets the deduction if it pays 75th-percentile wages and meets the health, pension, profit-sharing, and labor-neutrality tests, so automakers can simply skip the deduction and keep both the tax break's cost to the Treasury at zero and its benefit to workers at zero.
During the gap before new heavy-duty standards are written, the rules revert to the weaker 2016 Phase 2 standards.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The wage-deduction design is genuinely interesting: it ties a corporate tax cut to real, verifiable worker benefits rather than unconditional giveaway. But the conditions are voluntary, the cost to the Treasury is open-ended, and the bill's larger half — repealing the 2024 emissions and fuel-economy rules and ending California's stricter standards — shifts costs onto drivers and the public in the form of fuel spending and pollution. On balance the bill leans heavily toward manufacturers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced and has not moved since; no vote has been scheduled and the Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Troy Balderson introduced the Transportation Freedom Act on April 10, 2025, joined by Rep. Andy Barr.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee, the standard path for a bill touching both emissions rules and the tax code.
As of the latest action record, neither committee has taken it up — no markup, hearing, or floor vote appears in the history.
Sixteen members cosponsored the bill: 15 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has gained or lost yet. The 2024 emissions and fuel-economy rules remain in effect, and no tax deduction exists, because the bill has not advanced.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; current rules still stand

for.name: Troy Balderson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited cosponsors.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred, so the partisan shape is unknown; cosponsorship is mostly Republican but includes one Democrat.

industries.note: The bill hands them a doubled wage deduction and voids the 2024 emissions and fuel-economy rules they would otherwise have to meet starting with model year 2027. Part of the tax benefit is conditioned on paying high wages and providing strong benefits, but the deregulation half shifts costs to drivers and the public in fuel spending and pollution.
Weaker fuel-economy standards mean vehicles burn more gasoline, sustaining demand at the pump. Drivers pay that cost directly through higher lifetime fuel spending.
The Phase 3 heavy-duty greenhouse gas rules are repealed, and weaker 2016-era standards apply until new ones are written. The cost shows up as pollution from school buses and freight trucks.

The bill bars greenhouse gas standards from requiring electric vehicles and revokes California's zero-emission vehicle mandate, shrinking a mandated market for EVs and battery cells. Consumers lose the regulatory push toward cheaper-to-run electric cars but gain freedom from mandates.

industries.industry: California and other state air regulators
industries.note: The bill revokes California's Clean Air Act waivers, including the zero-emission vehicle mandate, and repeals the provision letting other states adopt its standards, ending their ability to set stricter rules than the federal government.

analysis.trajectory: Bills that sit in committee for months with only 16 cosponsors rarely advance on their own, and this one faces the added hurdle of splitting jurisdiction between two committees. The most realistic path for its provisions is absorption into a larger tax or reconciliation bill rather than standalone passage; if that does not happen, it dies when this Congress ends in January 2027.
